title: Beyond coverage: What digital inclusion really requires
snippet: Connectivity creates lasting value only when three conditions come together: people can reach it, the technology can understand them, and the services available through it allow them to do something meaningful The post Beyond coverage: What digital inclusion really requires appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
Contributed Article

By Jabbor Kayumov, Chief Executive Officer, Beeline Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan’s geography has always shaped its economics. It is the ninth-largest country in the world, with communities spread across vast steppe, desert and mountain terrain. For generations, distance has influenced the cost of connecting a clinic, a school, a farmer or a small business to markets and essential services.

Digital infrastructure is beginning to change the economics of that distance. But a signal bar alone is not digital inclusion. Connectivity creates lasting value only when three conditions come together: people can reach it, the technology can understand them, and the services available through it allow them to do something meaningful.

I lead Beeline Kazakhstan, and across my career with digital operators in Central Asia, South Asia and the Caribbean, I have seen very different markets confront the same challenge. Demand for digital participation almost always arrives before the infrastructure that enables it. A rural clinic, a family farm or a first-time online seller does not need to be persuaded that connectivity matters. They need access that is reliable, affordable and relevant to their lives.

The first requirement is reach

Terrestrial mobile networks will remain the backbone of connectivity. In Kazakhstan, Beeline has extended its network to villages with populations of around 100 people and has used solar power for base stations beyond the electricity grid. Yet in a country of this scale, the economics of a conventional tower will not close every remaining coverage gap.

That is why we are working with Starlink Direct to Cell to introduce satellite-to-phone connectivity in areas beyond the reach of terrestrial networks, beginning with messaging and expanding to data in a later phase, subject to the required approvals. The technology is designed to connect ordinary compatible mobile phones without a separate satellite terminal. It is not a replacement for terrestrial infrastructure. It is an extension of it, particularly where distance makes traditional deployment slow or uneconomic.

The real breakthrough will not be a successful demonstration. It will be a service that works reliably and can be sustained at scale. Technology must change not only the map of coverage, but also the economics of providing it.

The second requirement is relevance

Even universal coverage would be incomplete if the digital tools available through it could not properly understand the user’s language and context. Many of today’s leading AI systems perform best in languages with the largest digital footprints. Kazakh, like many national languages, remains underrepresented in the data on which global models are trained.

KazLLM is therefore more than a technical milestone. Developed through a national collaboration coordinated by the government and led by the Institute of Smart Systems and Artificial Intelligence at Nazarbayev University, with contributions from QazCode, Beeline Kazakhstan and Astana Hub, it gives developers an open-source foundation on which to build services in Kazakh. The larger point is simple: people should not have to leave their language behind to participate fully in the AI economy.

Compute capacity matters as well. Beeline Kazakhstan is building Hyper Cloud, a Tier III data center in Almaty targeted to come online by the end of 2026. It will provide domestic capacity for enterprise, cloud and AI workloads and help organizations keep sensitive data within Kazakhstan. The purpose of sovereign infrastructure is not isolation. It is the ability to participate in global technology with greater resilience, capability and agency.

The third requirement is utility

A connected person is not necessarily an included person. A signal reaching a remote community has limited impact if the person receiving it cannot open an account, receive a payment, access a public service, learn a new skill or sell a product beyond the local market. For a farmer, the value of connectivity may be payment for a harvest. For a small retailer, it may be accepting a digital payment without investing in expensive equipment. For a student, it may be accessing a course or paying a fee without traveling to a branch.

This is why connectivity, trusted digital identity, payment infrastructure and locally relevant services should not be planned as separate agendas. Each increases the value of the others. Kazakhstan’s work on the digital tenge is one example of financial infrastructure evolving alongside communications networks. The opportunity is to connect these layers so that access can translate into participation in the economy.

That also changes how we should think about investment. VEON has announced its intention to invest an additional $1 billion in Kazakhstan over the next three years. Capital on that scale must do more than add equipment. It should expand the number of people and businesses able to participate in the digital economy, strengthen domestic technological capability and create services that customers choose to use every day.

For that model to endure, inclusion must also be commercially sustainable. Remote communities cannot depend indefinitely on pilots or one-off interventions. Satellite connectivity can improve the economics of reach. Local-language AI can make technology useful to a wider population. Digital financial services can turn access into everyday economic activity. Built together, these capabilities reinforce one another.

Kazakhstan’s experience points to a broader lesson for other large and sparsely populated markets: digital inclusion must be built as a complete system. Reach without relevance leaves people behind. Relevance without useful services produces novelty rather than impact. And services without resilient infrastructure cannot scale.

Distance will remain a fact of Kazakhstan’s geography. It does not have to remain a limit on opportunity. If we build reach, relevance and utility together, a customer in a remote community is no longer at the edge of the digital economy, but fully part of it. That is the future we intend to help build.

Jabbor Kayumov was appointed Chief Executive Officer of Beeline Kazakhstan in April 2026.

Before his appointment, he served as Chief Executive Officer for the Telco Business at Beeline Kazakhstan. Prior to that, he held leadership roles across multiple international companies, including serving as CEO of Ncell in Nepal and leading Digicel’s operations in Jamaica and Trinidad & Tobago, where he oversaw their transformation into digital operators. He also served as CEO of Beeline Tajikistan. His leadership experience spans strategic transformation, commercial growth, organizational development, and digital innovation.

title: BT International adds security service edge to its Global Fabric
snippet: BT’s AI-ready networking platform now offers optimised connectivity to security service edge (SSE) solutions from Cisco, Fortinet, Netskope and Zscaler. The post BT International adds security service edge to its Global Fabric appeared first on Total Telecom.
fullText:
Press Release

BT International today announced the expansion of its Global Fabric network-as-a-service (NaaS) platform with a choice of security service edge (SSE) solutions to support multinational customers’ rapid deployment and scaling of AI agents, cloud applications and autonomous digital workflows.

As organisations adopt AI at scale, traffic patterns across the network are dramatically changing. A growing number of users, AI agents, applications and devices are demanding more bandwidth, lower latency and access to multiple clouds from more locations. Many CIOs now find that traditional network and security architectures lack the performance, scale, visibility and control needed to support these new demands.

By providing optimised connectivity between Global Fabric and SSE solutions from leading vendors Cisco, Fortinet, Netskope and Zscaler, BT International enables customers to select more predictable, high-performance routes for their traffic, improving application responsiveness and delivering the best user experience.

It does this thanks to Global Fabric’s cloud-centric architecture. Unlike traditional SSE deployments, where traffic may cross many third-party internet networks before reaching a security inspection point, Global Fabric provides optimised connectivity to the vendors’ security and cloud ecosystems at a choice of strategic cloud locations around the world.

The new capability extends Global Fabric’s growing ecosystem of networking, cloud and security services. It is the latest step in the expansion of the platform, which offers consistent security, optimised application performance and proactive network management in a single controlled environment built on a brand-new network underlay.

Yash Jethani, Principal Analyst, ISG, said: “The convergence of networking and security is ultimately about enabling trust at scale. Global enterprises increasingly require a cloud-delivered operating model that provides resilient connectivity, consistent security enforcement and simplified operations across users, applications, AI agents and digital ecosystems worldwide. The ability to deliver that trust consistently across markets will be a key competitive differentiator.”

Matt Swinden, managing director, strategy & product, BT International, said: “Agentic AI is changing what organisations need from networks. AI agents depend on secure, reliable access to applications, data and cloud services in real time, creating new demands for performance, resilience and security. By bringing together SSE with Global Fabric, we’re helping customers build an AI-ready network foundation upon which they can scale innovation and automation and choose the best security services to meet their needs.”
